extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting or analysing comparative historical narratives about civilizations (causes of progress/decline, cultural diffusion, institutions) for a general-reader textbook or survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached leisure class enables intellectual progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Phases of real intellectual progress in any community seem to be connected with the existence of a detached class of men, sufficiently free not to be obliged to toil or worry exhaustively about mundane needs, and not rich and powerful enough to be tempted into extravagances of lust, display, or cruelty. They must have a sense of security, but not a conceit of superiority. This class ... must be able to talk freely and communicate easily. It must not be watched for heresy or persecuted for any ideas it may express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells uses this as a general explanatory criterion for cultural/ intellectual florescence (examples: Athens, Renaissance Italy, the London Royal Society). The surrounding text emphasizes freedom from persecution, leisure from material toil, moderate social position (neither impoverished nor oligarchically rich), and freedom of communication as necessary conditions for sustained advances in philosophy, science, and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex writing systems constrain mass literacy and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The imprisonment of the Chinese mind in a script and in an idiom of thought so elaborate and so difficult that the mental energy of the country has been largely consumed in acquiring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells argues that an ideographic script (large number of complex signs) demands enormous time to learn, so only a small elite attain deep literacy; this filters out original, restive minds from positions of influence. He contrasts Mediterranean alphabets (easier to learn) with Chinese/Japanese systems and notes Korea's development of an alphabet and Japan's partial reforms. He also discusses dialectal variation as a practical barrier to phonetic reforms and mentions modern attempts at alphabetization and a 'standard Chinese' as a reform route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid examination systems suppress intellectual initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiarities of the Chinese script, and the educational system arising out of that script, must have acted age after age as an invincible filter that favoured the plastic and scholarly mind as against the restive and originating type, and kept the latter out of positions of influence and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells treats the imperial examination and its associated bookish training as an institutional mechanism that channels talent into conservative scholarly conformity rather than innovation. He explicitly calls the examination system 'rigid' and attributes to it the killing of 'intellectual initiatives' (noting later that it has been destroyed in modern reforms). Use this criterion when assessing whether an education/credential system fosters originality or conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material prosperity and contentment foster conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The very success and early prosperity and general contentment of China in the past must have worked to justify in that land all the natural self-complacency and conservatism of mankind. No animal will change when its conditions are 'good enough' for present survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general sociological principle Wells invokes: when basic needs and relative prosperity are met, societies and individuals have less incentive to innovate or undertake risky systemic change. Use this factor to explain cultural inertia even where capacity for invention exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic institutions (absence of abstract money/finance) promote stability
rubrics_metrics.description: China had no general coinage. The cash and credit system of the Western world, at once efficient and dangerous, had not strained her economic life... Wealth in China remained real and visible... No such development of 'finance' occurred in China. Wealth in China remained real and visible. And China had no need for any Licinian law, nor for a Tiberius Gracchus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells contrasts China’s material/land-based wealth and barter-like practices with Rome’s abstract monetary credit system to argue that the lack of abstract finance limited debt-driven social fluidity and therefore supported greater social stability. Use this criterion when evaluating how monetary and property institutions affect social cohesion and vulnerability to crises (e.g., concentration of debt, creditor classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of travel and communication accelerates diffusion of religions and ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: It is characteristic ... that Mani not only went about Iran preaching these new ... into Turkestan, into India, and over the passes into China. This freedom of travel is to be noted. It is interesting also because it brings before us the fact that Turkestan was no longer a country of dangerous nomads, but a country in which cities were flourishing and men had the education and leisure for theological argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells uses Mani’s and Yuan Chwang’s extensive travels and the arrival of Arab envoys in Canton as evidence that corridors of travel/trade and urbanized stops (cities with education/leisure) enable rapid east–west diffusion of religious and intellectual movements. Assess presence of trade routes, safe passage, urban centers, and patronage when judging potential for ideological spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural fusion of diverse influences can spark renaissances
rubrics_metrics.description: The renascence of China ... 'Four main factors had been brought together and fused: (1) Chinese liberal culture; (2) Chinese classicism; (3) Indian Buddhism; and (4) Northern bravery. A new China had come into being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells presents the Tang renaissance as an instance where the fusion of internal traditions with foreign ideas and martial elements produced a markedly new and vigorous civilization. When evaluating periods of rapid cultural/ artistic/ institutional renewal, examine whether multiple distinct cultural streams have been combined to create new syntheses.
